finds.quote: - The deixis-mechanism claim is **indexical, not allegorical**: κῆνος ὤνηρ as a demonstrative slot that transmission necessarily re-fills — every future receiver of the poem is *positioned* where the man sits, whoever the man "was." The girl need not be the poem; the mechanism operates at the level of deictic structure, not identity.
finds.note: The future-reader thesis: κῆνος ὤνηρ as a demonstrative slot transmission re-fills; argued here as distinct from Svenbro and Race; medium- and speaker-agnostic extension at 179–180.

finds.quote:
**Not found in the swept literature (the claimable wing, pending §7's sweep):**
1. κῆνος as **deictic transmission mechanism** — the demonstrative as an open indexical slot that every future receiver occupies by the poem's transmission, distinct from Svenbro's allegory and from Race's rhetorical-foil analysis.

finds.quote: Note the structural point for the piece: **the ancient record contains remembrance claims, not reader claims.** The reader enters by modern argument — via the literacy debate (fr. 147's "someone" as reader of a written text) or via Svenbro's allegorical reading of fr. 31. Keeping these two entry-points distinct is the single most clarifying move available.
finds.note: Thesis about what the ancient record does and does not contain.

finds.quote: So "some scholars believe" is Wikipedia compressing *the opposition as described by its opponent*. The CP piece can make this point with precision: the encyclopedia's authority chain for the future-reader-as-written-posterity claim runs through a single chapter that exists to refute it — and the actual bearers of the view are West and Parker, four and five decades old.
finds.window: reception: Wikipedia's Sappho article, Lardinois 2008, West 1970, Parker 1981
finds.note: Reception-history thesis about how the written-posterity view entered the encyclopedia; source-verified.

finds.quote: the deepest finding is structural: the future reader is not a theme that literature sometimes takes up. It is a position that writing as such creates, which particular traditions have made explicit, and which a small number of texts have *engineered*. Sappho 31, on the piece's reading, belongs to the last class — which is why the genealogy matters for the revision: it establishes what "engineering" means by contrast with mere address.
finds.window: the future reader from archaic epigraphy to the training layer
finds.note: Genealogical thesis: the future reader is a position writing creates; Sappho 31 among the few texts that engineer it; slot-building 'rarer, earlier' than explicit address (289).

finds.quote: - **Theognis 237–54**: the sphragis passage — I have given you wings, Kyrnos; you will be present at every feast, lying on young men's lips; and even in the future (καὶ ἐσσομένοισιν ἀοιδή...) you will be sung. The first *second-person* engineering of another's survival through song, with the poet's seal as authenticity device — transmission design avant la lettre.
finds.note: Priority-in-history claim: first second-person engineering of another's survival through song.

finds.quote: - **Ovid** — the decisive lexical step: *Met.* 15.878–79, "ore legar populi... vivam" — **"I shall be READ"**: the survival verb is now legere, not audire. The *Tristia* address readers to come directly from exile; the *Amores* and *Ars* cultivate the candidus lector. With Ovid the future reader is explicit, named, and relied upon.
finds.note: Thesis locating the transition from audire to legere at Ovid; borderline with established scholarship.

An extant Theophrastan work in which the fragment's aporiai are answered, making the fragment a Β to a Theophrastan Λ; none is extant. Or a collation of the fragment's text (Ross–Fobes, Gutas with the Arabic) that removes the hinge's wording; the paper's Greek is the seated First1KGreek text and awaits that collation.[^12]
finds.note: Historical thesis: the fragment is one work with Λ, divided by name; explicit falsifiers in §6.

finds.quote: An author's cut falls at a functional boundary. And this cut falls at the one sentence that changes the account's status: ἄρτιος ὁ λόγος under one name, λόγου δεῖται πλείονος under the other. Complete goes to the seal; needs-more goes to the draft. That is not where a partition would fall and it is exactly where a self-editing author would cut — the name changing at the point the function changes, and the hinge announcing both.

finds.note: Thesis on who divided the work: the seam's placement favours an author's editorial division over a librarian's partition.

finds.quote: The receiving texts describe the physical corpus as one lot: Strabo's τά τε Ἀριστοτέλους καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοφράστου βιβλία, sold together to Apellicon; Plutarch's τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν Ἀριστοτέλους καὶ Θεοφράστου βιβλίων, taken together by Sulla; and it was Andronicus, per Plutarch, who εἰς μέσον θεῖναι καὶ ἀναγράψαι τοὺς νῦν φερομένους πίνακας — *put them out and drew up the tables now in circulation*.[^10] The division of the one lot into two names is, on the receiving texts' own account, the editor's πίναξ.

deposits.genre_observed: philological theoretical paper with register counts on Theophrastus's Characters

finds.quote: Take the three modes not as authors but as operations indexed by names, each capable of recurring: the *Platonic* function dramatizes the problem in persons — scene, interlocutor, the definition sought; the *Theophrastan* function extracts, classifies, and registers — person and scene removed, type + definition + iterable deeds, the definition stated; the *Aristotelian* function organizes, explains, and architects — the type placed on a scale with its mean, cause, and exemplar, the definition explained.
finds.falsifier_quote: A genre would show the same marks wherever the genre appears, under any name. An operation indexed by a name would show its marks against the *same genre under the other name*. The proper control is therefore not the Ethics but *Rhetoric* II 12–17: Aristotle's own sketches of ἤθη — the young, the old, those in their prime, the well-born, the rich, the powerful — catalogues of characteristic behavior, the same kind of thing the *Characters* are.
finds.window: Theophrastus, Characters; Aristotle, Rhetoric II, EN II–IV; Plato, Republic VIII, Apology
finds.note: Thesis that the Characters' form is an operation of a named authorial function (the middle term), tested against Rhetoric II; results at 127.

finds.quote: **The one type that runs the whole line.** Irony. Dramatized in Plato as Socrates's method and his enemies' charge; catalogued in the *Characters* as the first vice, with ἀποροῦμαι in the list of evasions and no one inside it; theorized in the Ethics as the deficiency about truth, the more graceful end, οἷον καὶ Σωκράτης ἐποίει. One trait, three positions: person, sort, example. The *Characters* are the middle term of that sentence, and the sentence traverses three named authorial functions, read on a single word.
finds.note: Irony traverses three named authorial functions: person, sort, example.

finds.quote: Read as a receiving text, the preface is a *received character of the author* attached to a book of received characters: an aged sage, a dedicatee, a stated method, a pedagogic purpose — the colophon genre (Ep. II; the stone; the wills' Aristotle-image) performing its office at the head of the roll.
finds.note: Thesis about the prooemium's function as an author-frame supplied by the tradition.

finds.quote: Second, the Ethics' frame vocabulary is *EN*-specific — 12.76 in *EN* II–IV and below 0.6 in every other text measured, *Rhetoric* II and PA included — so the *Characters*' 0.15 is the ordinary absence of the Ethics' grid outside the Ethics, and an earlier inference from that count is withdrawn.[^5]
